#997. Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Some of Brazil’s wildlife have traces of plastic circulating in their blood — even if they live far from land used by humans, according to an analysis published on 11 November in Nature1.

Researchers measured the concentration of microplastics in the blood of 47 animals: 26 lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) and 21 giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla). The scientists found that, on average, the creatures carry similar levels of plastic as many humans — roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood. The animals that lived closest to human infrastructure and waste-management facilities had the highest levels of microplastics in their blood.

But even those living more than 100 kilometres from a waste sites and 65 kilometres from human infrastructure showed traces of the pollutants. This indicates that plastics can reach wildlife living far from where the pollution originates, says study co-author Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz, a conservation scientist at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus in Kelowna, Canada.

The findings are an important step to better understand how the particles impact wildlife, says Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou, a geochemist at the National Taiwan University in Taipei.

Microplastics are tiny particles (smaller than five millimetres across) with many different chemical compositions. They can travel through the environment in rainwater, rivers and the atmosphere. Although several studies have measured microplastics levels in wildlife, few have explored how the surrounding environment influences what animals ingest, says study co-author Michael Noonan, a quantitative ecologist at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus.

To find out, Noonan, Ferraz and their colleagues collected and analysed blood samples from animals living across the Amazon rainforest, the Cerrado savannah and the huge and pristine Pantanal wetland between February 2021 and November 2022. The researchers also used GPS data to track the animals’ movements and their exposure to a human footprint.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03660-5

Ferraz, M. A. M. M. et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x (2026).

#996. Cara Delevingne Has Advice for Single People Before “Tricky” Holidays

Cara Delevingne knows the holiday season can be tricky for single people, so she shared tips and tricks to avoid the holiday slump in an exclusive interview with E! News at GQ’s Men of the Year event.

Cara Delevingne is strutting into the holiday season with a game plan.

As Thanksgiving and Christmas fast approach, the British supermodel admitted this time of year “can be tricky,” especially for those who might be entering the holiday season single.

“It can bring around a lot of like, ‘Oh, my gosh, am I in a relationship? Is that lonely? Presents are expensive,’” Delevingne told E! News’ Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview at GQ’s Men of the Year event Nov. 12. “They can bring up a lot.”

Despite the holiday hubbub, though, the 34-year-old—who has been dating girlfriend Minke since 2022—emphasized ‘tis the season for rest and relaxation since we all “work too hard.” And that goes for everyone—despite relationship status.

“It's a time to have off, even if you're single, even if you're alone on the holiday,” she continued. “Find friends. Have Friendsgiving. Just find people. If not, catch up on the movies, watch TV shows.”

After all, a little R&R is how Delevingne has been leaning into the holiday season as of late. When the holidays kicked off not long after she began her sobriety journey in September 2022, she and Minke (real name Leah Mason) kept it chill that Christmas and New Year’s in Utah.

“It was just the two of us,” she told Vogue in March 2023. “I was in bed by 12:15 a.m. on New Year’s Eve having the nicest time.”

And since reconnecting with Minke in 2021—the pair had lost touch after attending grade school together in their teens—the Suicide Squad actress has found that she wouldn’t want anyone else by her side as she navigates her sobriety.

“These past two years have been A LOT of life. A lot of change, growth, pain and most importantly LOVE and I am so lucky to have found the perfect person to ride life’s ups and downs with,” Delevingne wrote on Instagram in 2022, celebrating their second anniversary. “I cannot imagine living life without you. I spent so long looking for my partner in crime, little did I know that it would be someone I went to school with (and had a baby gay crush on).”

Ahead of this holiday season, read on to look back at Delevingne through the years.

#994. How Sonia Bompastor’s ruthless changes inspired Chelsea’s win over Man City

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City: Sandy Baltimore’s stunning goal on the stroke of half-time condemned the champions to their first defeat of the season as the Blues replaced them at the top

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

On what ended up being an excellent day for Sonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager first had to accept that it started with a mistake. Kadeisha Buchanan, the centre-back, had been cleared to start by Chelsea’s medical team despite taking a knock to the head in training on Friday. Her assignment was to stop the world’s best striker, Khadija Shaw, who had arrived at Stamford Bridge having scored in nine Women’s Super League games in a row since the start of the season. But the way Chelsea set up in their top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City at first appeared designed to present Shaw with every opportunity to make it 10. For Bompastor, it soon became apparent that something was not right.

Buchanan, visibly struggling, was given a torrid opening 12 minutes, beaten for pace by Shaw twice on the outside and dragged into deeply uncomfortable positions as the striker roamed and bared her teeth. Aoba Fujino should have fired the champions in front after four minutes, but she placed Shaw’s cut-back horribly wide after Buchanan had been easily by-passed. Katie McCabe then had a narrow escape when she sliced Shaw’s cross past the post. Bracing herself on the touchline, Bompastor had to act.

The Chelsea back-line all looked up with the same blank expression as Veerle Buurman stood ready on the sideline; no one appeared to know the change that was coming. Buchanan, perhaps to hide her embarrassment, went straight down the tunnel. “Watching her from the beginning of the game, she was not 100 per cent,” Bompastor explained. “I know my player and she was not in the game. You have to be brave to make that change in the moment.”

Changing her back-line that early, Bompastor said, was a “risk”, but it was the ruthless change Chelsea needed. Bompastor spent the first half tinkering and tweaking until they could feel as if they could go toe-to-toe with Andree Jeglertz’s side. By the start of the second half, Chelsea had already made three changes. Buchanan’s early withdrawal was followed by Melvine Malard being forced off with a hamstring injury.

Sandy Baltimore’s stunning strike ended up being the winner, a thunderbolt that even she did not seem to expect, judging by the forward’s nonchalant celebration, but it was also her final touch as she was replaced at the break, as Bompastor decided to make a half-time change instead of using up her only available substitute window early in the second half.

That paid off, too. All the changes helped as Bompastor’s side began to compete and match City in all departments. Buurman was outstanding against Shaw and was not daunted to face her one-on-one. Lucy Bronze was immense, too, continuing to impress at centre-back and relishing the bruising battles with Shaw and Lauren Hemp. “They are magic and they can’t stop scoring,” Bronze said before revealing inspiration from McCabe. “We had to be dogs.” Eventually, Chelsea found a balance where they could be ferocious. Ellie Carpenter and Alyssa Thompson pushed high and wide, their midfield clicked together and City’s threat became muted; after such a menacing start, Shaw finished the game without a shot on target. “We restricted her,” Bronze added.

It meant Chelsea could leapfrog City to lead the WSL after 10 games, handing the champions their first defeat of the season while remaining unbeaten themselves. Despite the absence of Lauren James and their struggles to consistently turn chances into goals, they have found a way to win. Emma Hayes, the former Chelsea boss, ended the afternoon punching the air from her seat in the stands next to England manager Sarina Wiegman. This was a throwback to the Chelsea team she left, or the side Bompastor picked up in her first season at Stamford Bridge. “We’re in a better place than we were last year,” said Keira Walsh.

Jeglertz responded with his own changes and introducing the fit-again Vivianne Miedema and Laura Blindkilde-Brown almost turned the game in City’s favour. Hemp missed a sitter, inches away from the goal line, when the England winger failed to get a connection on Shaw’s lob. “We had a couple of great opportunities to score,” Jeglertz accepted. “We deserved more.” The second half had become breathless but City’s hopes were as good as over by the 75th minute when goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita was sent off for rushing off her line and clattering into Thompson after the winger had rounded her outside the box.

A City victory would have opened their lead in the title race to five points. For the first 10 minutes, the champions felt as if they would be leaving Stamford Bridge with a statement result. Instead, while London City Lionesses could enter the picture if they defeat Arsenal on Sunday, it is Chelsea who lead the way. Led by Bompastor’s example, their ruthlessness is back and they look up for the fight.

#993. Chacarra reveals plan for 'dream' win over McIlroy and 'Dubai double'

Rory McIlroy and Eugenio Chacarra sit four strokes back heading into the final day of the DP World Tour Championship; McIlroy needs solo fourth or better to have any chance of overtaking Chacarra in the Race to Dubai standings; watch live on Sunday from 6.30am on Sky Sports Golf

Eugenio Chacarra is eyeing more than just holding off Rory McIlroy to Race to Dubai victory at the DP World Tour Championship, following a strong finish to his third round.

Chacarra entered the week with a 533.93-point lead over McIlroy in the season-long standings, having won three times this year, only to lose ground with rounds of 72 and 71 over the first two days at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

McIlroy temporarily moved above Chacarra into projected top spot, as he chases a record-equalling eighth Order of Merit title, with the world No 2 also briefly jumping to the top of the leaderboard before stuttering to a third-round 72.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chacarra made nine birdies - including four in his last six holes - to post a four-under 68 and join McIlroy on five under, four strokes behind leader Tyrrell Hatton, but the Spaniard remains hopeful of challenging for tournament victory and 'Dubai double'.

"A lot of good and a lot of bad," Chacarra said about his performance. It has been a grind and I've been fighting. I've played all year on DP World Tour and I've played a lot.

"I want to really win that ranking, so I want to show the world I'm capable of playing under pressure. I think, so far, I've been doing that.

"I just want to win the tournament. I'm not far away. I know if I win the tournament, I win the ranking, so that's what I wanted to do in Abu Dhabi and I want to do it here.

"That's what we prepare for and I'm going to have a chance on Sunday. That's what we dream of since I was little is to win big events on Sunday.

"I'm ready. I love the game of golf. I love practising. I work so hard for these moments, and I'm going to go out there and enjoy it. Not a lot of people can enjoy this moment and have a chance to win the Race to Dubai."

Nine players started the week with a mathematical chance of topping the season-long standings, with South Africa's Jayden Schaper - needing a win and results to go his way - five strokes back and Jon Rahm a further shot behind.

McIlroy needs solo fourth or better to have any chance of surpassing Chacarra, who can guarantee the Order of Merit with victory, with the Spaniard still heading into the final round top of the projected Race to Dubai standings.

"There's a number of scenarios that could unfold tomorrow," former Ryder Cup captain Paul McGinley told Sky Sports. "I don't think Jon Rahm is not out of it yet - I could still see him coming through with a really strong last throw of the dice.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I think Rory [McIlroy] will reset and [Eugenio] Chacarra is going to battle some way or another. I don't think he's going to win the tournament, but he's going to really make it difficult for those guys.

"I think there are a few little things that can bob and weave there. At the moment, it does look like Chacarra is the favourite for the Race to Dubai. Rory has fallen a lot off the pace and it's going to take a big reset now for him tomorrow to really go at it and shoot a low score.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"McIlroy's still there, or thereabouts and he will reset overnight, so I expect a better Rory coming out tomorrow. If he can hit fairways, I think the rest of the game will be in good shape."

Starting the week 12th in the Race to Dubai standings and too far back to win the Harry Vardon Trophy, Hatton leads the tournament on nine under - one ahead of France's Victor Perez - as he looks to close out a ninth DP World Tour title.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It was a good day," said Hatton, a two-time runner-up at the DP World Tour Championship. "It was tricky - the greens were so fast on the back nine. Every putt I had coming in I think from the 13th was just unbelievably fast. Really happy with how I putted today.

"I know tomorrow is going to be a tough day. I've got enough experience down these last few holes to know that anything can happen. I'll just go out tomorrow and try my best. I know I can play well around here, and that's what I'll try to do."

Manchester United players will be put through their paces when Mauricio Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kyle Walker has revealed that Dele Alli was the only Tottenham Hotspur player he ever saw complete Mauricio Pochettino’s gruelling ‘Gacon’ running test during their time together in north London.

Pochettino earned a reputation in the Premier League for turning Spurs into one of the division's fittest, highest-pressing sides following his arrival from Southampton in 2014.

Speaking on The Overlap, a show brought to you by Sky Bet, Walker detailed the specific drill used by the Argentine coach to push his squad to their physical limits, and why it left such a lasting impression on the dressing room.

“We had the famous thing called the Gacon [running test] – whoever played for Tottenham will know the Gacon,” Walker said. “It starts at 145 metres and you have 45-seconds to get there, you then walk up five metres [to another cone] and have to run back. It’s a continuous thing and there were 16 or 17 cones.

“The only person that I’ve ever seen complete it was Dele Alli – he was an animal at running.”

Alli’s stamina was central to Pochettino’s blueprint at White Hart Lane during the mid-to-late-2010s. As the energetic attacking midfielder behind Harry Kane, Alli regularly covered more distance than any other player, led Tottenham’s counter-press and helped the club mount consecutive Premier League title challenges in 2016 and 2017.

The volume of endurance work under Pochettino became the benchmark for players to make the grade at Spurs, says Walker. So much so that when the right-back completed his £50 million transfer to Manchester City in the summer of 2017, the contrasting training methods under Pep Guardiola initially left him questioning his decision.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While Pochettino prioritised relentless off-the-ball running, Guardiola’s pre-season sessions revolved almost exclusively around possession drills, alongside relaxed training habits from some of Man City's senior stars.

“I remember getting off in the pre-season [at Manchester City] and you’ve got Kun Agüero who’s just balling around training – bad trainer, bad trainer but he turned it on in the game,” Walker explained.

“I got back to my hotel room after and speaking to my dad saying, ‘I think I’ve made a mistake here.’ I went from a [Mauricio] Pochettino team of running hard and we’re going to run all over you, dominating that area and also with a little bit of quality from certain players we’re going to win the game, to looking now and thinking we’re doing hardly any running in pre-season because Pep doesn’t like running – we did a little bit but it was mainly with the ball.”

Walker’s initial doubts quickly faded as Guardiola’s ball-dominant approach delivered several Premier League titles and a Champions League trophy during his spell at the Etihad Stadium.

However, with Pochettino set to make a return to English football at Manchester United, Walker’s recollection serves as a reminder of the intensity and demands the Argentine will expect of his new squad from day one.

Pochettino's first game in charge is expected to be Man United's visit to Anfield on November 22nd.

Manchester United have identified Nico Paz as the successor to Bruno Fernandes and the man to build their new team around.

That's according to a new report that puts the Red Devils in the midst of a bidding war for the Argentine superstar, with compatriot Mauricio Pochettino about to take the reins at Old Trafford.

Pochettino is stepping down from his role with the United States to become the eighth man to take the Manchester United job on a permanent basis since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 – and there could be a huge statement made in the market.

Bruno Fernandes has been arguably the greatest United buy of the post-Ferguson era, but after having the season of his life last term, the 32-year-old has shown his age this season, and FourFourTwo understands that for the first time, the Red Devils are starting to consider life beyond their talismanic captain.

While Pochettino is widely expected to build around the captain when he officially arrives through the door, Fichajes reports that United are one of a handful of European heavyweights vying to sign Como superstar Paz.

The outlet stars that the 22-year-old is seen as “a key figure to lead the team's rebuilding”, adding, “the club views him as a clear choice to replace Bruno Fernandes” – but it certainly won't be easy to lure him, with rivals able to offer more.

Premier League champions Arsenal are named among the suitors as they “see him as the ideal successor to Martin Odegaard”, with the 27-year-old Norwegian out of contract in 2028, while Chelsea are also mentioned in an ambitious plan to combine Paz with Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer.

Paris Saint-Germain are named as the final giant in the quartet to “intensify contact” with Paz and Como in December, though two stumbling blocks remain for all four in their bid to secure the playmaker.

When the Northern Italian outfit purchased Paz from Real Madrid, Los Blancos inserted an €80 million buy-back clause – and while Arda Guler and Jude Bellingham are currently shining at the Bernabeu, they also have a 50 per cent sell-on clause for any future deal.

This could drive the price up for Paz – along with any potential bidding war – with Como keen on receiving a £100m fee for a player they believe to be a generational talent.

United's pitch to Paz will surely centre on something that none of the other suitors can offer, however, in making him the face of their new project.

While Pochettino could well draw on coaching a fellow Argentine and note his excellent work in the past with the likes of Dele Alli and Cole Palmer at No.10, United have the space to allow Paz to flourish – if he is willing to take the huge leap to a side who are nowhere near competing for the biggest trophies at this moment in time.

The England and Arsenal midfielder, who has been accused of playing ‘old man football’, is only just returning to full fitness after a demanding season for club and country. By Miguel Delaney in Madrid

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As Declan Rice is discussing how he had an “average World Cup”, and talks at length about the challenges modern players have in ensuring prime fitness, a seemingly more trivial topic comes up: the punditry of Graeme Souness. The former Liverpool captain has in recent weeks criticised Rice for playing “old man’s football” and “cheating” in his midfield role, while insisting he’s a “centre-back”.

Rice, of course, handles it diplomatically – “there would be no disrespect there, I’d shake his hand, I’d chat with him” – but with some edge, too. The England vice-captain asserts this is what the modern game demands, and it’s completely different to Souness’ time.

“My numbers since I joined Arsenal speak for themselves,” Rice laughs, with a record of 15 goals and 25 assists in 129 Premier League appearances. “To be a top-class centre-back getting those numbers I’m delighted with that! The positioning, the ‘old man’s football’... look at Harry Kane. We played him the other week [a 2-2 Arsenal draw at Bayern Munich]. He dropped next to the centre-backs 20 to 30 times in the game to pick up the ball. The game’s different now.

“It's what the game demands, to get away from your man, to get away from who's marking you, to go into different areas to create overloads, to create two-v-ones, to progress the ball up the pitch. Football's way different. You're always trying to look for tactical advantages.”

Rice is essentially touching on a total transformation in football. Whereas “midfield generals” like Souness and even Roy Keane were able to fully impose themselves on a more loosely structured sport, their modern counterparts are now operating in a fully systemised game.

And yet the issue of movement, and even “old man’s football”, also touches on something that is a bit raw – literally. Rice admits he is still “building up to being a 100 per cent” following the World Cup, and that only comes after a necessary intervention involving Thomas Tuchel. The 27-year-old missed England’s last camp after coming off in Arsenal’s 3-0 defeat to Brighton – their only dropped points this season – and admitting he “did not feel right at all on the pitch”.

That came after a World Cup where he constantly suffered from hamstring pain, that radiated into his lower back, following a half-decade of constant football at the top level. “He [Tuchel] said, ‘Take some time, get yourself ready’,” Rice reveals. “It was using that time well to prepare to come back fitter, to come back stronger. It was always in my mind to be back ready for this camp. I am really happy and I am in a good place.”

Totally different to the World Cup, too, where Rice admits he was “annoyed” he couldn’t physically reach his best levels after a 69-game season for club and country, where he went from winning the Premier League and playing in a Champions League final to going straight into a World Cup. “I think by my standards it was an average,” he says. “It's annoying I couldn't perform how I did at Arsenal at the back end of the season.”

That is now the major challenge for players - and especially midfielders - of Rice’s level. They must balance having to play almost all the time, at a very intensive pace, with performance at elite level. That is not the easiest equation to solve, especially when you have numbers like an average of 64 games a season over five years.

“It is a tough one,” Rice acknowledges. “Last year I probably felt it more than anything in terms of the amount of games and the toll it takes on your body. I am realising as you get older you have to take the recovery side of it a lot more seriously. When you are 21, 22 and 23 you can get up and gallop around the golf course the next day. Even now I am young at 27, the demands of the game and all the competitions. You get up after a game and you feel your legs.

“It is not just the physical side, it is also the mental side. The pressure of delivering for a big club like Arsenal and being in every competition is the goal and we have built a squad where we can rotate but when you are playing well you don’t want to be dropped.”

Despite the workload, Rice doesn’t want to miss England camps, although one positive to being out of the last one was that he got to enjoy attending a first England game with his son, that 3-2 defeat to Spain. But the issue has become a theme over Tuchel’s time, as the coach has been big on commitment. That, nevertheless, is something the German would never question about Rice.

“I’ve always respected that,” he says. “I think, 82 caps, I’ve probably missed three camps in my time with England over an eight, nine-year period now. Last camp, if I didn’t speak to the manager about it, I wouldn’t have done it [dropped out]. But he gave me his word and we had a really honest chat about it, so I was in a better place mentally knowing that he authorised it.”

Rice’s respect for Tuchel is clear, to the point of making a huge claim: “Thomas is one of, if not the best man manager I've probably played under,” he says. “Just how he manages players, how he talks to players, how you can talk to him not just as a coach, but just as a person.”

Rice is happy to be back and England will need their vice-captain at his best if they are to beat the world champions Spain and qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners. “To beat Spain, as the away team, would be a massive thing for us,” he says. “The mindset is in a really good place, the manager’s messaging has been really good, so we need to go there and put on a performance.”

Perhaps Souness would approve, but Rice has his own high standards to meet.

#989. Aspyn Ovard Shares Devastating Details From Daughter’s Cancer Journey

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star Aspyn Ovard shared an emotional look at her 7-year-old daughter Cove’s years-long battle with terminal cancer: “Always racing against time.”

Aspyn Ovard is shedding light on her family’s heartbreaking journey.

After the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star publicly revealed her daughter Cove’s terminal cancer diagnosis on the Hulu series premiere, she shared further insight into the last few years of her life as she navigated the 7-year-old’s health battle.

“Almost 4 years and I still haven’t found the words to describe the pain,” Ovard wrote in a Nov. 13 Instagram post, which featured family photos from the past several years. “Our life ripped away.”

As the YouTuber—also mom to daughters Lola, 5, and Elle, 2, with ex-husband Parker Ferris—detailed the emotional toll of her daughter’s diagnosis, she shared photos of her baby girl in the hospital, cuddling up with her parents and celebrating her 4th birthday.

“Always advocating for my baby,” Ovard wrote. “Every hope and dream I ever had for my family is gone. I still haven’t found a way to cope.”

“Didn’t think she would get to turn 4,” she added. “Celebrated 3 more birthdays since, always thinking it’s the last.”

But amid Cove's health battle, the 30-year-old and her then-husband Ferris chose to expand their family.

Alongside a photo of her showing a growing baby bump, Ovard wrote, “Knew this was the right decision for our family even though I’d just decided to be done having kids days before diagnosis.”

And the reality star also went through another big change, explaining that she “said goodbye” to her “dream home” in Utah.

“My dream life didn’t exist anymore and I couldn’t live here,” Ovard wrote. “Hiding as much as I could. Tried to be normal online to keep one piece of my life consistent.”

But through it all, Ovard is continuing to cherish every single moment with her kids, as she shared a look into a past trip to Mexico.

“I’m always trying to make my little girl’s dreams come true,” she captioned a photo of her family with Paw Patrol characters. “Always racing against time.”

And experiencing the setbacks in Cove’s cancer battle doesn't get any easier for Ovard and her family, as she recalled one particularly painful memory when Cove was hospitalized two years to the day after being diagnosed. And the same nurse happened to be on shift during both visits.

“It was so triggering,” Ovard wrote alongside a throwback photo of her holding hands with Cove in the hospital. "Her face haunts me in the memories of the worst day of my life.”

While Ovard and her family try to stay strong amid the difficult journey, keep reading for a closer look at the cast of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County…

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, also share 8-year-old twins Luca and Rue.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

Madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that."

But, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives."

Avery Woods and David Woods, parents to Ziggy and Stevie, are still feeling the love after a decade of marriage. As she simply put it, "my forever + always."

Ex-Southampton and Manchester United midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin backs one player in particular to benefit from Mauricio Pochettino's coaching

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Manchester United and Southampton midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin believes Mason Mount has the right profile to flourish once Mauricio Pochettino takes charge at Old Trafford.

With Pochettino set to be confirmed as Michael Carrick’s successor following Thursday’s dismissal, Schneiderlin has backed the 27-year-old to become an important figure in the Argentine’s rebuild.

Man United have reportedly agreed a two-and-a-half-year contract with Pochettino, paying roughly £7 million in compensation to release him from his post with the United States national team.

Pochettino will inherit a side languishing 18th in the Premier League table, ahead of a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on November 22nd.

Having played the best football of his career under Pochettino at St Mary’s, Schneiderlin is convinced Mount’s work rate and technical ability will quickly earn the new head coach’s trust.

"Mason Mount is definitely that type of player and profile that Mauricio Pochettino likes very much," Schneiderlin said, via Comeon.com.

"I think he will do great under him. He loves players who don't have big egos, who work hard, and have quality on the ball. They can really develop under him."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Pochettino's arrival at Chelsea in the summer of 2023 coincided with Mount's switch to Manchester, as the England midfielder sought a new environment. However, injuries and managerial upheaval have stalled his progress at Old Trafford since. Restricted to a 25-minute substitute appearance in last Sunday’s chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, the midfielder will now be presented with a fresh opportunity to establish himself.

Schneiderlin also highlighted Youri Tielemans, who arrived at Old Trafford from Aston Villa in a £35 million summer move, as another midfielder capable of thriving under the Argentine, pointing to the balanced partnership he formed with Victor Wanyama under Pochettino on the south coast.

"Youri Tielemans is someone who also has legs and great quality on the ball and so he gives you different options, and of course, look at my partnership with Victor Wanyama," Schneiderlin added.

While Pochettino’s teams are synonymous with high-intensity pressing, Schneiderlin stressed that his former manager isn't just a coach who likes to fill the pitch with runners. At Southampton, Wanyama anchored the midfield while Schneiderlin pushed forward - a method Pochettino can replicate at Man United by pairing deeper ball-winners like Carlos Baleba alongside progressive passers such as Tielemans, Bruno Fernandes, or Kobbie Mainoo.

"Victor was more of a midfielder who sat a bit deeper and was very strong physically," Schneiderlin explained. "Pochettino doesn't just need players with huge engines who run, run, run. He knows how to adapt to the specific characteristics of his players."

With minimal time on the training pitch between arriving in Manchester next Wednesday and facing Liverpool four days later, Pochettino’s priority will be stabilising a porous side. If Schneiderlin’s assessment proves accurate, Mount’s energy and tactical flexibility could be key to dragging the club clear of the relegation zone.

#986. Trafford to start in Spain - but what are Tuchel's other selection issues?

Key selection issues analysed ahead of England's Nations League clash with Spain in Madrid; Three Lions will win Group A3 with victory over world champions; Follow Spain vs England in our live blog on the Sky Sports website and App on Sunday, kick-off 7.45pm

Football Correspondent @RobDorsettSky

Against the best team in the world, Thomas Tuchel's defensive decisions will be key. And he has many to make.

The England head coach said before Croatia at Wembley on Thursday that he was quite happy to go full-strength in both matches, despite the three-day gap, and he was true to his word. All the big guns were out for Harry Kane's big night.

Barring unexpected late injury or illness, the best player in the world will lead the line against the world champions. Morgan Rogers should start at right wing, Anthony Gordon left wing. England's Madrid maestro Jude Bellingham will play No 10, and Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice will form the double pivot.

But behind that is where Tuchel and his assistant Anthony Barry will be pondering their options.

Tuchel answered the biggest selection question 24 hours before kick-off, announcing James Trafford will start over Jordan Pickford against Spain in Madrid.

"Trafford will play tomorrow," confirmed Tuchel. "We want to see how far Traff is.

"We give him the opportunity, which is rare. We use the Nations League for that, to see him and trust him in a high-pressure match."

The decision could be one of the most important we have seen for eight years. Since the 2018 World Cup in Russia, Pickford's consistent brilliance means he largely been unchallenged as England's first-choice goalkeeper. Not now.

As he nears his century of international caps (Pickford has 94), Trafford has emerged as the new pretender to his throne. In the last international camp, Tuchel shared the four games equally between the two and he will do the same this time round.

Seeing Pickford walk out at Wembley on Thursday, in the lesser of the two matches, was a surprise. Most onlookers expected him to get the nod against the world champions in Madrid.

But Tuchel has stuck to the plan he outlined at the start of the camp and brought Trafford in. It feels like a real changing-of-the-guard moment for the England No 1 shirt.

In terms of outfielders, no decision is bigger than who should play left-back, to try to combat the most potent of Spain's threats, Lamine Yamal. The man who finished third in the Ballon d'Or rankings stayed in Barcelona for treatment on a troublesome right knee rather than travelling to Prague on Thursday night. He was being saved for England and he is fit and back with the national team now.

Most likely, Lewis Hall will be given the task of keeping Lamine Yamal quiet, keeping his place on the left side of England's defence. Tuchel said after his performance against Croatia that Hall is "doing all he needs to do" to nail down the role as England's first choice and that he is playing "top level".

The Newcastle defender has already proved himself against Barcelona's wondrous winger. In the spring of this year, in the Champions League, he put in a performance that led the Spanish-based newspaper Mundo Deportivo to label Hall the "anti-Lamine".

On the other side of England's defence, it feels like a straight shoot-out between Ben White and Djed Spence, with Trent Alexander-Arnold no doubt expecting to be dropped. Tuchel has consistently questioned his defending and so he is likely to sit out the test in Spain.

Spence missed two England training sessions and Thursday night's game against Croatia as he nursed himself to be ready for this one. He was one of England's most formidable finds of the World Cup, proving himself to be the team's best one-on-one defender.

White has only started one game for his country since before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and that was the 1-0 home defeat to Japan. If he does get the nod over Spence, both he and Tuchel will hope he avoids the boos which marked his substitute appearance against Croatia on Thursday night.

Alex Baena, who is likely to be Spain's left winger, doesn't pose the same threat as Lamine Yamal on the other flank but he did score against Czech Republic a few days ago - and against England at Wembley.

In the centre of England's defence, again, Tuchel has some big calls. If Ezri Konsa, rested against Croatia, is now fully fit, as he seems to be, he will almost certainly be recalled straight to the heart of the defence. In the absence of the injured Marc Guehi and John Stones he is England's most senior and most influential defender.

Jarell Quansah, who had a howler for Croatia's equalising goal, may well drop out because he is considered a right-sided centre-back, as is Konsa. So that would mean the left-leaning Dan Burn or Jarrad Branthwaite coming in alongside the Arsenal man. Best bet there is Burn.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Significantly, Trafford was the preferred choice when Tuchel's men played Spain in September.

For that reason, and also because this is England's final game of 2026, and because it is their last until the Nations League quarter-finals in March - it feels a hugely significant match.

The animosity from large chunks of England's support, and from some England players, towards Tuchel for those now infamous tactical choices of the World Cup semi-final against Argentina, have melted away. The national team's autumn performances have reignited hope and belief.

Which way the result - and the performance - goes against the World Cup winners, will almost certainly dictate the mood and the direction of travel for England from here on in.

In the persistent rain of Madrid, the game will be a barometer of where England are, in project Thomas Tuchel 2.0.

#985. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

Ex-Premier League boss Sam Allardyce is not known for couching his opinions and he has strong feelings about the fallout at Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Premier League manager Sam Allardyce believes Michael Carrick’s dismissal at Manchester United has all but ended his coaching career, while accusing the Old Trafford dressing room of 'shafting' their former boss.

Carrick was relieved of his duties on Thursday after a dismal opening to the 2026/27 campaign had left Man United sitting 18th in the table with just one win in 10 matches.

Speaking to Boyle Sports and Footy Accumulators’ No Tippy Tappy Football podcast, Allardyce suggested the 45-year-old has neither the financial need nor the appetite to step back into a dugout following consecutive difficult exits at Middlesbrough and Old Trafford.

“I don't think Michael Carrick will manage at all again – I think this will have finished him,” Allardyce said. “I think he'll be saying, 'I'm not bothered with any of this now.'

“It wasn't great, what happened at Middlesbrough, was it? And Michael Carrick, in his position, doesn't need another job in management, financially. He'd only need to do it if he wants to go out and prove people wrong if he gets the opportunity again. But he may well just choose to slip away quietly.”

While Man United’s hierarchy pulled the trigger to pave the way for Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment, Allardyce insists the board showed patience and instead has laid the blame at the feet of the squad.

“The Manchester United board gave him as long as they could. But the players have shafted him,” he added. “You can't play for that man as well as you did last season and then give up on him for whatever reason.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I don't know what's caused the turnaround, but he'll have an idea why the squad is not as good as when he finished last season.”

Allardyce also identified what he believes were issues in Carrick’s midfield setup, arguing that playing summer signing Youri Tielemans alongside Kobbie Mainoo left the team far too easy to bypass in transition.

“Tielemans and Mainoo can't play together because they can't run,” Allardyce explained.

“They can run, but not quick enough. That brings criticism from all the punters. But I'll tell you why they don't do more: because they can't. They physically can't.”

Pochettino will inherit a fractured squad next week ahead of a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in what will be his first game in charge.

Allardyce’s verdict highlights the scale of the overhaul awaiting the incoming Argentine, and ultimately the heavy toll the Old Trafford job may have taken on Carrick.

#983. Dept. Q Crew Member Dies on Set in Edinburgh

A crew member of the Netflix series Dept. Q, which films in Edinburgh, Scotland, died while on set Nov. 12, according to Left Bank Pictures, the production company behind the show.

Tragedy has struck the set of popular Netflix series Dept. Q.

Left Bank Pictures, the British production company that produces the series, confirmed that an unnamed crew member died while on set Nov. 12.

“We are deeply shocked and saddened by the tragic death of a member of our Dept. Q crew,” a company spokesperson told E! News in a Nov. 13 statement. “Our thoughts are with their family, friends and colleagues at this incredibly difficult time, and we are offering support for those affected.”

Left Bank Pictures—behind other series like The Crown and Outlander—had recently wrapped season two at FirstStage Studios in Edinburgh when the incident occurred, according to local police.

“Around 3 p.m. on Thursday, 12 Nov., 2026, we were called to a report of a man seriously injured at an industrial premises in the Bath Road area of Edinburgh,” a Police Scotland spokesperson told local outlet The Edinburgh Reporter. “Emergency services attended, however, the man was pronounced dead a short time later.”

Amid the tragic death, authorities added, “The death is not being treated as suspicious, however, inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances.”

E! News has reached out to the Edinburgh Police Department but has not yet heard back. Netflix referred a request for comment to Left Bank Pictures.

In 2022, a crew member named Philip Ross also died while on site at FirstStage Studios. His death is still the subject of a Fatal Accident Inquiry by local authorities, according to multiple outlets.

“FirstStage Studios was devastated to learn of the tragic death of a contractor working for one of our production customers,” the company shared in a 2022 statement. “We understand an investigation is under way so cannot comment further save to offer our condolences to the contractor’s family and colleagues.”

Starring Matthew Goode, Leah Byrne, Jamie Sives and Alexej Manvelov, Dept. Q follows a detective who works to solve a cold case while processing a recent personal tragedy. Season one premiered in May 2025.

#981. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

#976. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."

The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.
